result.reading: Straight after the outburst of block 3, where he wants to fling the windows open and throw the people out with the rubbish, this one-line question drops from rage to a plea: having no one around him is the good he longs for and cannot get. It turns the refrain of blocks 1 and 2, where he twice says he cannot have that condition, into a prayer addressed to no one, and the exclamation about waiting in block 5 carries the longing on. The rest of the story answers it: the escape to the empty green country (9–13), the moment he is finally alone in the dark house (14), his self-mockery that he wanted silence and an absence of people and now has them (16), and the crowd of the dead who come anyway (17–18).

elements.where: the one-line question in which he asks who will grant him the condition he longs for: what that condition is, and whether he wants the condition itself or comfort for it
elements.what: The noun and the infinitive phrase together name the gift he asks for. Having no one around him is itself the relief and pleasure he craves after blocks 1–3, where people crowd into him like travellers into an inn. The adjective names that plain condition, the one he wants. It does not mean the ache of missing company, which is its other everyday sense. A fast reader who takes the noun as comfort for a sorrow and the adjective in its sad sense turns the line into a man asking to be consoled for his isolation. That reverses the story, where people are the torment and their absence the cure.

checks.ask: Is the condition of being alone itself the good he longs for here, the thing that would bring him relief?
checks.fail: The line asks to be comforted or consoled in, or for, his being alone, so solitude becomes the trouble rather than the wish.

checks.ask: Is the condition named without the sense of being unhappy for lack of company?
checks.fail: It is named with a word that, said of a person, normally means unhappy at being without company (for example 'lonely' or 'loneliness').

elements.where: the condition he asks to be granted in this one-line question, set beside what he twice says he cannot be in blocks 1 and 2
elements.what: The phrase repeats word for word the refrain of blocks 1 and 2, where he twice declares that he cannot have this condition, each time beside the complaint that he cannot get out of people's way. Here the refrain comes back as a plea. The story later grants it and mocks it. In block 14 he at last has it, alone in the dark house, and the original uses the same root there. In block 16 he taunts himself that he wanted silence and an absence of people and now has them. A reader of the original hears this line as the third sounding of the refrain.

checks.ask: Is the condition he longs for here named with the same key word or root that the translation uses in blocks 1 and 2 for what he says he cannot be? If those two blocks differ from each other, matching either is enough.
checks.fail: The key word here differs from the one in blocks 1 and 2, so the refrain is not heard. For instance, one place speaks of being alone and the other of solitude, privacy, peace or being by oneself. Whether the word wrongly suggests sadness is judged under E1b, not here.

elements.where: the framing of this one-line plea: whom it turns to for the thing he longs for
elements.what: A plea put as a question about who might bestow something out of reach is the optative formula of the Church Slavonic Bible. Ukrainian readers of the time knew it from the Psalter and the prophets. In Psalm 55 (54 in Slavonic numbering) the psalmist longs for a dove's wings to fly from the violence and strife of the city and be at rest. In Jeremiah 9:2 the prophet longs for a wayfarers' lodging in the wilderness so that he could leave his people, while the narrator of block 3 complains that he himself has become such a lodging for crowds. The line therefore sounds like a psalmist's lament, which suits a story about fleeing the city for empty green country to rest. Because the giver is no one in particular, the question also implies that no one will grant it.

checks.ask: Is the condition framed as something an unnamed someone would have to give, grant or allow him, that is, an appeal to an outside giver as in the scriptural formula?
checks.fail: The line becomes his own plain wish, exclamation or statement with no giver at all (a longing, a hope, an if-only), or it is put to a particular person, so the appeal that carries the scriptural echo is gone.
